title: Conjecture 1.1
statement_text: If any connected component of $G$ is not a complete graph, then $\chi_{ISC}(G) < \chi_{SC}(G)$.
context_text: A function $f:V(G)\to\mathbb{N}$ is a choice function for $G$ if $G$ has a proper colouring from the lists $L$ whenever $|L(v)|\ge f(v)$ for every vertex $v$; the sum choice number $\chi_{SC}(G)$ (Isaak) is the minimum of $\sum_vf(v)$ over choice functions. The interactive sum choice number $\chi_{ISC}(G)$ is defined by a game: all lists start empty; in each round Alice chooses a vertex $v$ and Bob adds to $L(v)$ a colour not already in it; the game stops as soon as $G$ has a proper colouring from the current lists, Alice trying to minimise and Bob to maximise the number of rounds; $\chi_{ISC}(G)$ is the number of rounds under optimal play. Clearly $\chi_{ISC}(G)\le\chi_{SC}(G)\le|V|+|E|$, the latter being the greedy bound; graphs attaining it are called sc-greedy. Equality $\chi_{ISC}=\chi_{SC}$ holds for complete graphs (Bob gives colours $1,2,\dots$ in order at every vertex), and hence for disjoint unions of complete graphs, while for example $\chi_{SC}(P_3)=5$ but $\chi_{ISC}(P_3)=4$. The authors confirm the conjecture for all sc-greedy graphs and show that the gap $\chi_{SC}-\chi_{ISC}$ grows with the number of vertices (in many cases linearly) for trees, unbalanced complete bipartite graphs and grids.
notes: Source is PDF; the conjecture statement itself contains only simple inequality notation and is cleanly readable.
paper_title: The Interactive Sum Choice Number of Graphs
